topic: What if you opened a McDonald's in ancient Rome?

script.text: First, you need a kitchen. And it turns out Rome already has fast food. All over the city, there are little street counters with big clay pots sunk into the stone, selling hot food to people whose apartments don't even have kitchens. In Pompeii alone, archaeologists have found about eighty of them. That's real.
One of those counters, right next to the giant race track called the Circus Maximus, belongs to a widow named Tullia. Business is terrible. Her son Felix is sweeping an empty floor.
You unwrap your cold burger and cut it into three. Tullia chews. Felix chews. Silence. Then Tullia rolls up her sleeves.
Building a burger in Rome is harder than it sounds. Bread is easy. The bakers here make beautiful loaves. You just ask for them round. Cheese? Rome loves cheese. Lettuce and onions? No problem.

The meat is trickier. Cows here pull ploughs, so you use pork. Then Tullia shows you an old recipe. Minced meat, pepper, pine nuts and fish sauce, pressed into a patty. A Roman cookbook really has one. That's real. Rome basically invented the burger. It just forgot the bun.

Ketchup is impossible. Tomatoes come from the Americas, and nobody will bring them to Europe for another fourteen hundred years. Same with potatoes, so no fries. You try turnip fries instead. Felix spits his into a pot.

But your real secret isn't the food. It's the system. One grill. One job per person. A painted menu with pictures, because a lot of people here can't read. Clay tokens with numbers, so nobody fights over whose order is next.

You set the price at two bronze coins. In Pompeii, a cup of wine cost one. The first day, you sell forty burgers. The third day, four hundred. By the end of the week, the line goes around the block, and a gladiator asks if he can marry Tullia.

science.claim: In Pompeii archaeologists have found about eighty street food counters (thermopolia).
science.working: The Pompeii Archaeological Park put the number of thermopolia found in Pompeii at about 80 when it unveiled the Regio V thermopolium in December 2020.
science.source: Parco Archeologico di Pompei, press release on the Regio V thermopolium (26 Dec 2020); BBC News, 'Pompeii: Ancient Roman street food counter unearthed' (Dec 2020)

science.claim: Many Romans lived in apartments without kitchens and ate at street counters.
science.working: Most insulae flats had no proper kitchen; cookshops and thermopolia fed them.
science.source: Smithsonian Magazine, 'Pompeii's Snack Bar' (2020); M. Beard, 'Pompeii: The Life of a Roman Town' (2008)

science.claim: A Roman cookbook has a minced-meat patty with pepper, pine nuts and fish sauce.
science.working: Isicia omentata in the Apicius collection (De re coquinaria, book 2): minced meat with pepper, pine nuts, garum and wine, shaped and wrapped in caul fat.
science.source: Apicius, De re coquinaria 2.1; Smithsonian / BBC coverage calling it 'the Roman burger'

science.claim: Tomatoes and potatoes reached Europe only after 1492.
science.working: Both are American crops brought to Europe in the 16th century; 1492 - 64 = 1,428 years, 'fourteen hundred years'.

science.claim: In Pompeii a cup of wine cost one as.
science.working: A bar inscription in Pompeii (CIL IV 1679): 'For one as you can drink wine; for two, the best; for four, Falernian.' The as was a bronze/copper coin.
